content: The systematic reviews were developed by the respective reviewers with input from the World Health Organization (WHO). Drafts were shared for feedback, and the final outputs were thoroughly discussed with the methodologist to ensure they were appropriately formatted and interpreted for use in the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting. The GDG made the final decisions regarding the overall GRADE certainty rating for each PICO question by evaluating the consistency of critical outcomes. They selected the highest rating when results were consistently beneficial across outcomes or the lowest rating when results were inconsistent. The systematic review and meta-analysis led by the Medical University of South Carolina, USA, included five studies (data from 10 articles and 8 conference abstracts), comprising one Phase IIb safety study, two randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and two open-label extension trials. The search spanned from January 1, 2010, to August 3, 2020, and utilized databases such as PubMed, CINAHL, and EMBASE. Another systematic review and meta-analysis, led by the Global Health Impact Group Team in Atlanta, USA, identified seven studies, including two RCTs and five cohort studies. The search covered January 2014 to August 2020 and included databases such as PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane CENTRAL, EMBASE, CPCI-S, and WHO Global Index Medicus. A third systematic review and meta-analysis, led by the University of Cape Town, South Africa, included 35 studies (three systematic reviews on test accuracy, 29 original research reports from 28 studies, and three programmatic reports). Clinical data were reported in six publications and one conference poster, including one RCT, two non-randomized studies, and four single-cohort studies. The search extended through August 2020 and utilized databases such as PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Registers, WHO Global Index Medicus, and conference databases. The PICO question addressed whether the HIV viral load testing algorithm outlined in the 2016 WHO guidelines should be modified. Subquestions included: (a) whether the first viral load test should be conducted 1 or 3 months after ART initiation instead of 6 months, (b) whether repeat viral load testing for elevated levels should occur earlier (1 month later versus 3–6 months later), (c) whether individuals on efavirenz-based ART with elevated viral loads should switch immediately to second-line ART without repeat testing, and (d) whether the viral load treatment failure threshold should be lowered from 1000 copies/mL. Supportive evidence reviews were conducted for these subquestions, led by the Global Health Impact Group Team, with searches spanning January 2005 to June 2020. The systematic review for subquestion (a) included eight RCTs among adults and two RCTs among children, along with an observational study on advanced HIV disease. For subquestion (b), 25 studies were summarized (20 retrospective and 5 prospective), mostly involving adults, with one study on adolescents and two on children. For subquestion (c), 31 studies were included, with 16 focusing on virological failure or disease progression, 8 on drug resistance (cohort studies), and 7 on HIV transmission. For subquestion (d), nine national surveys on acquired drug resistance among adults, one systematic review (66 studies), and one prospective cohort study were included. The WHO commissioned a global survey on feasibility, acceptability, values, and preferences, distributed to people living with HIV, healthcare workers, and program managers. Despite low response rates, the results were analyzed by a qualitative scientist. Feasibility evidence was identified for point-of-care infant diagnosis, viral load testing, and treatment-monitoring algorithms, including the use of dried blood spots and point-of-care testing with lower thresholds. Incremental costs for point-of-care device placement were evaluated, and an affordability analysis was conducted in selected countries. The Guideline Development Group met virtually via Zoom from September 28 to October 2, 2020, to finalize updated recommendations. Participants registered in advance and identified themselves as GDG members. A 60% majority vote was agreed upon for decision-making if consensus was difficult, but all recommendations were ultimately formulated through consensus. Systematic reviews and evidence-to-decision-making tables were shared in advance and presented during the meeting, with discussions facilitated by the methodologist. The WHO ensured transparency and addressed conflicts of interest. All external contributors completed a declaration of interests form, and a web-based search was conducted to identify potential competing interests. Conflicts were reviewed by the WHO Guideline Steering Group, and management plans were developed. One GDG member declared a potential conflict of interest and recused themselves from decision-making for a specific recommendation. No other conflicts warranted exclusion from discussions. The draft guidelines were circulated for peer review to GDG and External Review Group members in November 2020. External reviewers signed confidentiality agreements, and their comments were considered during the review process.
